*Phase 0: Collecting Humans Before You Have Anything to Offer Them*

On Wishonia, if someone discovered everyone was dying from preventable causes, they would simply stop dying from preventable causes. On Earth, you need a tax-exempt entity, a bank account, and written permission from something called the Securities and Exchange Commission before you're allowed to try. The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates securities, which are financial instruments, not the kind of security where people stop dying. That would be a different department. You don't have that department.

So you can't accept money yet. You can't sell bonds yet. You can't do anything that involves the movement of small pieces of paper. What you CAN do is collect names. The goal of Phase 0 is building a database of every human who agrees that dying from preventable causes is a strange thing to tolerate. It's a Kickstarter where the reward tier is "possibly not dying," which is the most compelling crowdfunding offer in history, and yet somehow requires marketing.

## The Bureaucratic Nesting Doll Problem

On your planet, before you can accept donations, you need 501(c)(3) status. Before you can sell bonds, you need SEC registration. Before you can do either, you need a bank account. Before you can open a bank account, you need an organization. Before you can have an organization, you need the bank account. It's like a door that requires a key that's locked inside the room the door opens to. Your species built this system on purpose.

The solution is the same one humans have used every time this has happened, which is every time. You collect people first, then point at the crowd when the institutions ask "but who wants this?"

Abolition started with a list of names. Suffrage started with a list of names. Civil rights started with a list of names. Someone wrote down who agreed. The names became a number. The number became bargaining power. The bargaining power became policy. Then the policy became a holiday, and everyone pretended they'd agreed all along. Your species does this every 40 years and never recognizes the pattern.

## Three Types of Humans Who Want to Help

People who agree with "dying is bad" fall into three categories.

### Spreadsheet Humans (Investors)

These are humans who hear "{{< var victory_bond_annual_return_pct >}} annual return on [Victory Incentive Alignment Bonds](/knowledge/solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) [@iab-paper-2025] backed by redirected military spending" and immediately open a spreadsheet. Their pupils dilate. Their pulse quickens. They ask about the term structure. Then they ask about the term structure again. Then they ask a third question, which is also about the term structure.

These humans are not broken. They are simply running financial software on moral hardware. They process "millions of people are dying" faster when it arrives formatted as a revenue projection. They'll wait years for a good investment to materialize. They will not wait thirty seconds for a bad one. If your math is solid, these humans will follow you to the gates of hell, provided the risk-adjusted return on entering hell is competitive.

Do not try to make them cry. Make them calculate. Crying is temporary. Compound interest is forever.

### Heart Humans (Advocates)

These are humans motivated by the mission itself. They share things on social media, write letters to politicians, volunteer time, donate money they probably shouldn't, and cry at commercials about dogs. They are, frankly, the only reason your species has ever improved anything. Without them, the spreadsheet humans would still be optimizing returns on the slave trade.

The critical mistake every movement makes with these humans is telling them to "care about this" without giving them something to do. I have watched 4,297 years of humans being told to "raise awareness." The awareness has been raised. It's been raised so many times it has a penthouse suite. Nobody told it what to do next.

Give heart humans a button. Give them a form. Give them a link to share. Give them a specific politician to call and a specific sentence to say when they call. If you give a human a feeling without an action, you haven't recruited a supporter. You've manufactured a sad person. Your planet has enough of those.

### Institutional Humans (Partners)

Organizations (nonprofits, research institutions, health agencies) that already work on pieces of this problem. They have infrastructure, credibility, and mailing lists. You have a framework that could make their existing work more effective. This is a trade, not charity. Approach it like one.

What you're offering: money, without a grant application. (Grant applications are documents in which humans spend 200 hours explaining why they deserve money, so that a committee can spend 40 minutes deciding they don't. It's your species' least efficient art form.)

One warning: institutions are territorial in the way that dogs are territorial, except dogs eventually stop barking. Two nonprofits working on the same disease will fight each other harder than they fight the disease. This is called "the nonprofit sector." Approach each one as if they are the only organization doing this work. They already believe this, so you're just agreeing with them.

## Phase 0: The Shopping List

By the end of Phase 0, you want:

- **100,000+ registered humans** who typed their name into a box indicating they prefer living. This sounds like it should be everyone, but on your planet, "dying is bad" is apparently a niche political position that requires organized support.
- **1,000+ spreadsheet humans** with stated investment ranges (how many papers they'd give you, if you were allowed to accept papers, which you're not yet, but you're writing it down for later)
- **100+ institutional humans** with expressed interest in collaborating (or at least not actively opposing you, which on your planet counts as enthusiasm)
- **{{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}}+ in stated investment demand** (registered, not committed; this is humans saying "I would give you this many papers" without actually giving you the papers, which your species calls a "letter of intent" and treats as meaningful)

This database is your ammunition for every bureaucratic nesting doll that follows. When you apply for 501(c)(3) status, you point at the list and say "here are our supporters." When you file SEC registration, you point at the list and say "here is market demand." When you meet politicians, you point at the list and say "here are your constituents." When you launch, you point at the list and say "here are your users."

Bureaucrats don't respond to arguments. They respond to evidence that other people already responded to arguments. They say "how many people already think this is a good idea?" and then, if the number is large enough, they act as though they thought of it themselves. Nobody admits this because admitting it would require a committee to approve the admission.

## Getting Started (It Takes Twenty Minutes)

1. **Build three boxes where humans type their name to indicate they prefer living.** One box for spreadsheet humans (asks: how many papers would you invest?). One box for heart humans (asks: what skills do you have? how many hours per week?). One box for institutional humans (asks: what does your organization do? how many people does it reach?). This takes twenty minutes. Your species spent longer than that choosing the name "Department of Defense" for a department that mainly attacks people.

2. **Put up a website.** The three boxes and the argument. It does not need to be pretty. No movement in history was stopped because the font was wrong. The suffragettes did not fail to get the vote because their pamphlets used Comic Sans. (Comic Sans didn't exist yet, which is the only reason they didn't. Your species would absolutely have used Comic Sans on suffrage pamphlets.)

3. **Start telling other humans.** Social media, Reddit, forums, conferences, your dentist. Especially your dentist. You're already trapped in the chair. They can't leave either. Their hands are in your mouth. It's the most captive audience in human civilization. You're not going to get a better recruiting environment than a room where both parties are contractually obligated to remain in close proximity and one of them is holding sharp instruments.

4. **Send monthly updates with real numbers.** "3,247 registered investors representing $180M in stated investment demand" beats "the movement is growing!" in the same way that "your tumor is 2.3 centimeters" beats "your health situation is evolving." Adults prefer arithmetic to enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is what humans feel before they do math. Arithmetic is what humans feel after. Both are useful. But only one of them convinces spreadsheet humans, and you need the spreadsheet humans because they have the papers.

## The Comforting Asymmetry

The military-industrial complex has a 65-year head start, unlimited budgets, and thousands of professional persuaders. You have a spreadsheet and an argument.

Historically, that's been enough. Every major social change in your species' history was started by someone with less money, fewer connections, and worse odds than the thing they were trying to change. Abolitionists were outspent by slave owners by a factor your calculators would refuse to display. Suffragettes were outspent by the entire concept of patriarchy, which didn't even need a budget because it was just how things were. Civil rights activists were outspent by the governments actively trying to kill them.

They all had the same thing you have: an argument that was obviously correct, and enough humans willing to write their names down.

It shouldn't work this way. Spreadsheets, budgets, and lobbyists should always beat arguments and names. But your species is weird like that. You're the only civilization I've observed where being right occasionally defeats being rich. It happens rarely, and it takes too long, and it requires an embarrassing amount of suffering first. But it happens. And it starts with a list of names.

## The Question You Can't Answer Wrong {#logical-inevitability-theorem}

Before we get to the part where you copy, paste, and send, there's a sequence of questions you should walk anyone through. Each question is individually undeniable. The sequence is inescapable. On Wishonia, we call this "conversation." On Earth, you call it the Socratic method, because you named it after the one guy who did it and then you killed him.

Here are the questions. Try to answer any of them wrong.

**Question 1: Is it physically possible?**

Among the near-infinite solution space for human action, is there *some* action, *somewhere*, that could improve how your species allocates resources toward ending war and disease? Or is the current allocation, where you spend {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} a year on weapons and {{< var global_government_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} on clinical trials, the theoretical optimum? Is this the best any civilization could possibly do? Your species spends {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}} times more on weapons than on clinical trials. If someone told you their household spent {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}} times more on swords than on medicine, would you say "that sounds optimal" or would you say "are you okay?"

Nobody will say it's physically impossible. Saying "there is no possible improvement to resource allocation" is the intellectual equivalent of saying "this is the best of all possible worlds," which is a position held by exactly one fictional character invented specifically to be wrong.

**Question 2: What does the solution look like?**

If optimal allocation existed, what would a world with compounding benefits look like? If you redirected even 1% of military spending to medicine that works and let it compound for 20 years, the models show everyone could be {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} richer. Not metaphorically richer. Not spiritually richer. Richer in the way that involves having more money. The compounding math is in the [GDP Trajectories](/knowledge/economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd) [@gdp-trajectories-paper-2025] chapter and it is not subtle.

**Question 3: Do you have a better approach?**

Is the [1% Treaty](../solution/1-percent-treaty.qmd) [@1-pct-treaty-impact-paper-2025] the least bad approach, or do you have a superior one? This is not a rhetorical question. If you have a better plan, the authors of this manual would genuinely like to hear it. They will switch to your plan immediately. They have no attachment to this specific mechanism beyond the fact that nobody has proposed a better one. If your alternative is "do nothing and hope," that is not a plan. That is what you've been doing. The results are in.

**Question 4: Should this be your top priority?**

If ending war and disease is physically possible, and the result is {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} more resources for *everything*, then persuading those with sufficient power to implement it should temporarily be your top priority. Not because you're altruistic. Because it gives you that many more resources to achieve whatever your *actual* goals are. If someone offered to multiply your budget by that much in exchange for a few years of focused effort, and you said "no thanks, I'm busy," you would not be principled. You would be bad at math.

**Question 5: Then what are you waiting for?**

If ending war and disease is physically possible, and all humans would benefit unimaginably from it, then you don't need to persuade anyone to be altruistic. You need to get the argument in front of one credible, self-interested actor with enough capital and legitimacy to trigger the financing mechanism. In practice, that means one person who can publicly underwrite the assurance contract, fund the initial bonus pool, and make everyone after them feel less crazy. In a world where that person understood the compounding benefits and the mechanism, the end of war and disease would not require heroism. It would require arithmetic.

That is the bottleneck. Not generic "awareness." Not funding in the aggregate. Not human nature. The bottleneck is that nobody with a large enough checkbook has read this yet. The entire apparatus of self-interest is sitting there, ready to work, waiting for one public commitment that has not happened yet because someone in the chain decided they were "busy."

On Wishonia, this sequence of logic doesn't have a name, for the same reason gravity doesn't have a marketing department. On Earth, you apparently need to brand obvious things before your species will take them seriously, so: **The Logical Inevitability Theorem.** If an optimization is physically possible, and its benefits compound for all participants, then the decisive trigger is one informed self-interested first mover making a credible public commitment. After that, it spreads. That's it. That's the theorem. Five sentences. On Wishonia, this is considered too obvious to state. On Earth, it's considered too idealistic to believe. One of these planets cured disease. The other one is still arguing about it.

On Wishonia, the Logical Inevitability Theorem would take about four minutes to demonstrate and the conversation would end with both parties agreeing to stop wasting money on murder. On Earth, it takes four minutes and the conversation ends with one party saying "interesting, I'll think about it" and then never thinking about it. This is the coordination failure the entire manual is about. You are not reading about it. You are currently doing it.

### The Zero Percent Problem

Most humans do not refute novel proposals. They round them down to zero and call that discernment.

But **0% is not a mood. It is a claim.** To assign literal zero probability to this plan, you need to assert at least one of the following:

1. Better global resource allocation is physically impossible.
2. No way of paying people could ever change politics.
3. This specific mechanism has a fatal flaw you can name.

If you are not claiming one of those three things, then your actual estimate is not 0%. It is "I have not evaluated it." That is a different sentence. And once the probability is above 0 by any nontrivial amount, forwarding it to one capable evaluator becomes the rational move. The cost is trivial. You are not being asked to believe. You are being asked not to disguise unexamined dismissal as analysis.

### How Trivial, Exactly

On Wishonia, "the cost is trivial" would be sufficient. On Earth, your species requires a number.

Forwarding takes roughly 30 seconds. The average human earns {{< var global_avg_hourly_income >}} per hour. That makes the opportunity cost of sharing approximately {{< var sharing_opportunity_cost >}}. The upside, if the treaty path works, is {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in additional cumulative lifetime income for the average person (from the compounding math in [GDP Trajectories](/knowledge/economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd)); {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_multiplier >}} their current trajectory. (If you earn more than the global average, your personal gain is proportionally larger.)

The upside exceeds the downside by a factor of {{< var sharing_upside_downside_ratio_treaty >}}. Which means sharing is irrational only if the probability of *any* improvement to global resource allocation is less than 1 in {{< var sharing_breakeven_one_in_treaty >}}.

To put that in perspective: the probability of being struck by lightning in a given year is about 1 in 1.2 million. You would need to believe this plan is roughly 200 times less likely than being struck by lightning. Not "unlikely." Not "a long shot." Two hundred times less likely than a thing that actually happens to real humans every year.

And note what "this plan working" requires you to deny. The five questions of the Logical Inevitability Theorem:

1. **Is better resource allocation physically possible?** To get below the breakeven threshold, you'd need to believe it is physically impossible to improve on a system that spends {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} per year preparing to kill people and {{< var global_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} per year trying to cure them.
2. **Do the benefits compound?** You'd need to believe that redirecting resources from destruction to medicine produces zero cumulative economic or health gains over 20 years. Not small gains. Zero.
3. **Is there a less-bad approach?** You'd need to believe that no incentive-compatible mechanism, out of all possible mechanisms, could ever motivate any political shift. Not this specific mechanism. Any mechanism.
4. **Does this dominate alternatives?** You'd need to believe that no reallocation of military spending has ever worked, despite your own species cutting military spending by 87% after World War II and experiencing the largest economic boom in human history.
5. **Is the only bottleneck informed self-interest?** You'd need to believe that no self-interested actor (billionaire, sovereign wealth fund, or government) would ever act when the return on investment is {{< var treaty_roi_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}} to one, even when the structure pays them to do so.

To clear the breakeven threshold, you don't need to believe all five. You need to believe *any one of them* is not impossible. That's it. One non-zero answer out of five, and sharing becomes the rational move.

And this calculation is conservative. It counts only the income gain. It assigns zero value to the {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} lives. It ignores the [Wishonian](../futures/wishonia.qmd) [Optimal Governance Trajectory](../economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd) entirely (which is {{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_multiplier >}} the current trajectory, not {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_multiplier >}}). It assumes you personally capture only the average gain, when in practice higher earners gain proportionally more. The actual breakeven threshold is even more forgiving than 1 in {{< var sharing_breakeven_one_in_treaty >}}.

On Wishonia, a species that couldn't clear a 1-in-{{< var sharing_breakeven_one_in_treaty >}} bar for obvious self-interest would be a genuinely novel research subject. We have never encountered a species that fails to act on incentives this large. We don't have a word for it. The closest translation is "sleeping through your own house fire, but on purpose."

### The Only Remaining Failure Mode

So: better resource allocation is physically possible. The benefits compound. No better mechanism exists. The precedent is real. The incentives pay. Sharing costs 30 seconds and is rational at any probability above 1 in {{< var sharing_breakeven_one_in_treaty >}}.

The math can't be wrong. The incentives can't fail. Selfishness can't stop it; selfishness is the engine. The only thing that can kill it is you not reading this far and then not pressing "send." That's it. The entire distance between here and the treaty is made of humans who couldn't pay attention for five minutes.

I have watched 420 civilizations go extinct. Every single one had the math. None of them could pay attention long enough to do the cost-benefit analysis.

## Your Ammunition (Copy, Paste, Send) {#your-ammunition}

You've read the plan. You've seen the math. You can't give the information back.

So consider your situation. There are four outcomes:

1. You forward the message below to the most powerful person you know, and the plan works. You are in the causal chain that saved {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} lives.
2. You forward it, and the plan fails. You lost 30 seconds.
3. You do nothing, and the plan would have worked. You chose 30 seconds over {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} lives.
4. You do nothing, and the plan wouldn't have worked anyway. Nothing happens, except you're the kind of person who picked "nothing" when "30 seconds" was also available.

Forwarding dominates not-forwarding in every scenario. This is not an opinion. It's a payoff matrix. On Wishonia, choosing option 3 or 4 when option 1 costs 30 seconds would not happen, because it doesn't make sense, and on Wishonia things that don't make sense don't happen. On Earth, it happens constantly. You call it "being busy."

The payoff matrix above is denominated in lives. Your species has difficulty acting on lives. (You tolerate {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} preventable deaths right now, and your primary response is to feel briefly sad about it.) So here is the same calculation in the unit that actually moves humans.

Even just the treaty path alone (redirect the murder budget, fix nothing else) produces an economy {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} larger than the baseline by year 20. Not a little larger. {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} larger. This compounds over 20 years, which is the part that makes the number large and the part that makes delay expensive. Over an average remaining lifespan, your cumulative earnings under the treaty path would be {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_multiplier >}} what they'd be on the current trajectory. For the average human, the gain is {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in additional lifetime income. If you earn more than the global average (and if you're reading this on a device that costs more than most humans earn in a month, you do), your personal gain is proportionally larger.

The opportunity cost of not forwarding is not "30 seconds." It is {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in foregone lifetime income for the average person, compounding over {{< var global_avg_remaining_years_nounit >}} remaining years. Each year the treaty hasn't started is a year the 20-year compounding clock hasn't started. On Wishonia, failing to start this clock would be considered so strange that nobody would believe you if you described it. On Earth, it is called "Tuesday."

On Wishonia, the payoff matrix would be sufficient. On Earth, your species apparently needs to formalize obvious incentives into binding contracts before it will act on them. Fortunately, your economists already invented one. It's called a dominant assurance contract. Here's how it works: a contract operator sets a threshold and a failure bonus, then a credible anchor investor publicly underwrites the thing so everyone else can see the first real money on the table. After that, you pledge to support the treaty, conditional on enough others pledging too. If the threshold is met and the treaty works, you receive a tiny fraction of the value created. (A tiny fraction of "everyone is {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} richer" is still a lot of money.) If the threshold isn't met, you get your pledge back plus a bonus for having tried. Once the structure is credible, participation becomes the rational move. You profit if it works. You profit if it doesn't. The only way to lose is to not participate, which is the position you're currently in.

This is not a new idea. Your economist Alex Tabarrok formalized it decades ago. It solves exactly the problem this chapter diagnoses: everyone waits because everyone else is waiting. A dominant assurance contract makes waiting the only irrational option. It turns "someone else will do it" from a comfortable excuse into a financial mistake. The [Victory Incentive Alignment Bonds](/knowledge/solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) chapter explains the specific instrument. The assurance contract is just the mechanism that gets enough humans to say "yes" at the same time, which is the part your species is bad at.

The ask is not "share with a friend." Friends are horizontal. The ask is: forward to the most powerful person you know who plausibly has a checkbook, public credibility, or direct access to someone who does. Because that person knows someone more powerful than them, and that person knows someone more powerful than them, and so on. If each recipient forwards to one person more powerful than themselves, the message reaches someone who can trigger the plan in roughly 15 to 20 hops. Not mass adoption. Not "raising awareness." One chain, climbing. If each person forwards to just one person, every human on Earth has the information in 33 steps. You don't need step 33. You need the step where it reaches the first credible anchor investor.

Below is the message. Copy it. Paste it. Send it. Then there are five variations for different kinds of humans.

Not because you caused them, but because you now know about a plan to prevent them and must actively choose not to act. You cannot un-read this. The plan: redirect 1% of military spending to clinical trials. The math: {{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}} per year of life saved. The podcast is 5 minutes. Forward this to the most powerful person you know, or live with the arithmetic.
>
> [manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/podcast](https://manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/podcast)

### Which Message for Which Human

Not all humans respond to the same logic. This is inconvenient but predictable from a species that can't agree on pizza toppings.

- **The most powerful person you know:** Send [**The Message**](#the-message). It combines every mechanism into a single inescapable sequence. This is the one you send when you have one shot.
- **Spreadsheet humans** (engineers, economists, EA people): [**Spreadsheet Humans**](#for-spreadsheet-humans). The 2x2 payoff matrix. They'll verify it. They won't find a flaw. They'll forward it because the math says to.
- **Skeptics who reflexively say "0%"**: [**Skeptics Who Round to Zero**](#for-skeptics-who-round-to-zero). It forces them to justify literal impossibility instead of hiding behind dismissive vibes.
- **Contrarians and people who think of themselves as brave**: [**Contrarians**](#for-contrarians). Daring them not to forward it is more effective than asking them to forward it. Reverse psychology works on exactly the humans who insist reverse psychology doesn't work on them.
- **Legacy-anxious humans** (founders, executives, anyone who's ever used the phrase "my impact"): [**Legacy-Anxious Humans**](#for-legacy-anxious-humans). They're already worried about how history will judge them. Give them something specific to worry about.
- **People who've read the manual**: [**People Who Read the Manual**](#for-people-who-read-the-manual). It mirrors the manual's own thesis. Not forwarding it literally proves the manual right about them.
- **Everyone else**: [**Everyone Else**](#for-everyone-else). Simple, self-contained, hard to argue with.

## The Horizontal Path: The Most Important Secret in the World {#the-horizontal-path}

Everything above this section describes the **vertical** strategy. You forward the plan up the chain. Human to more-powerful human. After 15 to 20 hops the message lands on the desk of an anchor investor. They trigger the financing mechanism. It works if any link does their job.

The failure mode is simple. Somewhere in the chain, one human is busy. Busy is contagious. The message dies in an inbox next to a dry-cleaning reminder.

What follows is the **horizontal** strategy. It runs in parallel. It assumes the chain does not find its anchor in time. Or that the anchor wants to see public demand first. Humans with checkbooks like receipts.

So: instead of one climbing message, you run a doubling wave. Everyone calls two people. Those two call two. And so on. Until the visible vote count at [warondisease.org](https://warondisease.org/) is too large for any government to politely ignore.

The vertical path looks for a key. The horizontal path builds a crowd. Your species has confirmed, experimentally, about seventeen times in the last century, that crowds above a certain size make buildings open on their own.

### The Script

You message someone you love. You say, with complete sincerity:

> "Either I am crazy or I have discovered the most important secret in the history of the universe. Can you call me and tell me which?"

Then you tell them. The 1% Treaty exists. Redirecting one percent of global military spending into clinical trials produces {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_nounit >}} times more trial capacity. That compresses the timeline for eradicating the major diseases from centuries to decades. (The math is in the [1% Treaty Impact](/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd) paper and the [Parameters & Calculations](/knowledge/appendix/parameters-and-calculations.qmd) appendix.)

In concrete terms. "Centuries" means the cure for your specific disease is discovered posthumously. By your great-great-grandchildren. Who do not know which ancestor it was for. "Decades" means the cure is discovered while you are still alive to take it.

You and everyone you love die of disease on the long timeline. You and everyone you love live longer on the short timeline. The difference is whether the treaty exists.

The cost to them is thirty seconds at [warondisease.org](https://warondisease.org/), plus doing this exact same thing for everyone they love.

That is the entire script.

### Why This Framing Works (The Attention Problem)

Most arguments fail not because they are refuted but because they are never evaluated. Attention is finite. Defaults are powerful. Your species has evolved a set of efficient heuristics for ignoring novel claims, and those heuristics fire before any evaluation happens. The claim never reaches the cortex. It bounces off the reflex.

The "either I am crazy or..." framing solves this specific problem. It bypasses the reflex long enough for the argument to get a hearing. A human who has called back to judge whether you have lost your mind has pre-committed to at least sixty seconds of genuine attention. That is the entire window you need. Sixty seconds is enough to state the treaty, the math, and the ask. After that, the argument either stands on its own or it does not, but at least it was evaluated.

The usual "can I tell you a secret" opener pattern-matches to pyramid schemes, cult recruitment, and multi-level marketing. The self-deprecating version does not, because pyramid schemes do not open with the possibility that the pitcher is mentally ill. That is the only thing a pyramid scheme will never say about itself. Using it as your opener is counter-signaling: you are telling the recipient that you are pre-committed to accepting their negative verdict, which is exactly what a scheme-runner cannot do.

On Wishonia, we do not have a word for "refusing to evaluate an argument because it pattern-matches to arguments you have previously refused to evaluate." The closest translation is "being asleep on purpose." The sanity-check framing is the alarm clock.

### The Math: Thirty-Two Doublings to Four Billion

If every person persuades two new people, and each doubling takes roughly one week, then reaching {{< var global_coordination_target_supporters_nounit >}} supporters requires about 32 doublings. That is 32 weeks, which is under eight months. If the doubling cadence is one day instead of one week, it is 32 days. The math is not subtle. 2 to the 32nd power is roughly 4.3 billion. Your species invented this math. You just rarely apply it to yourselves.

No real-world cascade has ever held a clean doubling for 32 generations. Saturation happens. Message fatigue happens. The second call reaches someone who already got the call. The realistic curve is logistic, not exponential. It flattens well before 4 billion.

For reference. Your most successful religious movements took millennia. Your viral pet videos plateau at a few hundred million. This plan completes faster than religion. And is harder to get wrong than a pet video.

But note what the logistic curve actually implies. It implies that the ceiling is not a technical limit; it is a friction limit. Every unit of friction you can remove (a clearer script, a shorter URL, a more compelling framing) raises the ceiling. You do not need a clean doubling. You need enough doublings for the visible vote count at [warondisease.org](https://warondisease.org/) to cross the threshold where governments respond. That threshold is unknown but finite. And every month the wave propagates, {{< var global_disease_deaths_per_minute_nounit >}} humans die per minute from the diseases the treaty would accelerate the cures for. The clock is running whether you make the call or not.

### The Pascal Objection (and Why It Collapses Here)

A philosopher will object that this is Pascal's Mugging. The structure is: someone presents an astronomical payoff, probability-weighted by a small credence, and demands you act because the expected value is large. Rational agents rightly resist this reasoning, because if you accept it once you must accept it for every claim of the form, and there are infinitely many such claims.

But Pascal's Mugging usually asks you to give a stranger money, or do something unpleasant, or violate a strong prior. The canonical cases involve paying ten dollars to avoid an asteroid only the stranger can see. The cost side is real, the payoff is speculative, the structure is predatory.

The 1% Treaty ask is different in every dimension. The cost is calling someone you love and having a meaningful conversation, which is not a cost at most humans would recognize as one. The mechanism is not speculative; it is the boring kind of policy change (redirecting a tiny fraction of a budget line) that has precedent (the 87% post-WW2 reallocation documented in the [Peace Dividend](/knowledge/economics/peace-dividend.qmd) chapter). The payoff is not Pascal's cosmic reward; it is compounding GDP growth and fewer dead relatives, both of which your species already believes in.

The break-even probability for the individual sharing decision, derived in [The Zero Percent Problem](#the-zero-percent-problem) above, is {{< var sharing_breakeven_one_in_treaty >}} to one. Below that probability, sharing is irrational. Above it, sharing dominates. Your actual credence does not have to be high. It has to be higher than being struck by lightning 200 times. If you cannot clear that bar for a plan your own planet's history contains a precedent for, the problem is not the plan.

Your species has placed larger bets on homeopathy. Homeopathy has no mechanism. No precedent. You bet real money on that. We are asking for a phone call.

### The Dominance Argument

Construct the two-by-two.

- If you make the call and the plan works: you participated in compressing the timeline for disease eradication by centuries. You are in the causal chain of {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} prevented deaths.
- If you make the call and the plan fails: you had a meaningful conversation with someone you love about something you care about. This is the cost.
- If you do not make the call and the plan would have worked: you chose "nicer to not seem weird on the phone" over {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} lives.
- If you do not make the call and the plan would not have worked either way: nothing happens, except you are the kind of person who picked "nothing" when "call someone you love" was also available.

This is not an expected value argument. It is stronger. An expected value argument says one option has higher probability-weighted payoff. A dominance argument says one option is better in every scenario. Making the call dominates not making the call. The only scenario in which you are worse off for having made the call is the one where the conversation itself was bad, and the conversation is "I wanted to share something important with you," which is not a bad conversation in any culture your species has produced.

On Wishonia, the observation that one option dominates the other is considered sufficient justification for taking that option. On Earth, it is considered interesting but not motivating. I continue to find this difference confusing.

### The Uncomfortable Implication

Once you have done the reveal (told your person about the treaty, asked them to vote at [warondisease.org](https://warondisease.org/), asked them to do the same for everyone they love) the clock starts on what happens next.

If the causal chain holds (and you believe the [1% Treaty Impact](/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd) analysis, which computes roughly {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_nounit >}} times more trial capacity at 1% reallocation), then every minute you continue talking to this one person instead of calling the next person is a minute during which {{< var global_disease_deaths_per_minute_nounit >}} more humans die of preventable causes, somewhere on the planet. The math is indifferent to how much you love the person you are currently talking to.

Which means any additional conversation after the reveal is a choice. Specifically, it is the choice to value the present conversation above the suffering that the delay causes. This is not a wrong choice. It might be the correct choice. Loving the person in front of you more than the statistical humans you will never meet is how your species survived long enough to build clinical trials in the first place. The implication is not that you should stop talking. The implication is that once you have had the reveal, every further minute of the conversation is a deliberate act of love, not an absent-minded default. Both of you get to feel this. It is a strange and intimate thing to notice together.

On Wishonia, shared awareness of a secret this size would be treated as one of the high forms of friendship. Your species has not invented a word for it yet. You should.

### The Script (Copy, Send, Then Use What Follows When They Call)

**The opener (message this):**

> Either I am crazy or I have discovered the most important secret in the history of the universe. Can you call me and tell me which?

**How many people should you send the opener to?**

Everyone you love. For most humans that is around forty people (close family, closest friends, a few meaningful coworkers, your one friend from college you still talk to). Not 150; 150 is Dunbar's cap for stable relationships, which includes people you would not call about anything important. "Everyone you love" is a smaller, realer circle. Forty is an estimate of the size of yours. If yours is larger, call more.

**Do not stop early.** For the wave to reach four billion voters, each caller needs exactly two contacts to *actually continue the chain* (call their own loved ones, run the script, etc.). Conversion rates for close-contact political asks run between five and ten percent in the published literature on viral civic campaigns. At ten percent, twenty calls nets two propagators; at five percent, forty calls nets two; at worse rates, you need more. But the deeper problem is that you cannot verify which calls netted propagators. Verbal commitment is not action. Humans agree on the phone and then get busy, forget, or let the social moment pass. You will never find out which of your contacts actually ran their own calls. The only protection against that drop-off is volume: every additional call you make increases the probability that *at least two* produced real propagation, even if several promised and did not deliver. Stopping at two verbal commits is how the chain silently dies. Target everyone.

**How to actually do forty calls: one per day.**

Forty calls is not something a human does in one sitting. Make the first one the moment you finish this chapter. Momentum matters more than rate. Every hour you delay the first call is {{< var global_disease_deaths_per_minute_nounit >}} times 60 humans.

After that, set a daily alarm. Or a recurring calendar event. One call per day, every day, for about six weeks. This is the pace at which you will actually do it. Faster: you burn out. Slower: the wave decelerates.

Daily alarms beat willpower. Willpower depletes. Alarms do not. Let the alarm have the discipline. You just answer it.

**Accept that most of them will not act, and reframe the call anyway.**

About ninety percent of your contacts will not take real action, regardless of what they say on the phone. This is the published base rate for political asks, and the chain model already accounts for it. You are not trying to convert everyone. You are trying to propagate through the statistical minority who will. If you expect enthusiastic yeses and get polite nods, you will quit after five calls. If you expect ninety percent polite nods and count any genuine propagation as a gift, you will finish the list.

Because most of your calls will feel like pleasant conversations that do not obviously produce action, reframe each one. You are not making a pitch. You are using a real argument as the excuse to spend a few minutes with someone you care about and tell them, out loud, that you do not want them to suffer and die of diseases that are basically solvable engineering problems. That is a good use of a phone call regardless of what they do next. If they also vote and recurse, the wave advances. If they do not, you still told someone you love that you love them, using the clearest and most specific language your species has available for that claim, which is "I do not want you to die of something fixable." The conversation itself was worth having. Forty of those conversations is, by most human metrics, a good month.

**What is actually happening when you make these calls.**

Two waves propagate at once. The first is horizontal. Each contact who acts recruits their own contacts. Until the vote count at warondisease.org is too large to ignore.

The second is vertical. You do not have to aim for it. Social networks have hubs. The person in your life who knows a senator. The senator who knows a president. A horizontal wave of forty calls eventually touches a hub. The hub becomes a vertical channel. The message routes upward as a byproduct of propagating sideways.

You do not have to know a powerful person. You have to call forty people you love. The network does the upward routing for you. Within a handful of hops. Your LinkedIn connections are not qualified for this work. The network is. At no charge. Without caring whether you notice.

Your message probably reaches a head of state well before it reaches four billion voters.

**Send your personal referral link, not the bare URL.**

After you vote at warondisease.org, check whether the site gives you a personal referral link. If it does, that link is what you send to the people you call, not the bare domain. Two reasons. First, the referral link carries your identity, which lets the chain be traced. You can see how many voters your calls produced, and so can every caller below you in the recursion. The count becomes legible, which makes the project feel real instead of theoretical. Second, there is a prize pool under development. It would pay voters a share proportional to the size of the chain they seeded. Payable after the treaty passes. The design is not final. No guarantees. But if it lands, the referral link is how you qualify. If you care about the optional upside, use the referral link. If you do not, the bare URL still works for the vote.

Your species, when offered "base case" versus "greedy case," picks greedy. Every time. No reason to break the streak for this one.

**When they call, walk them through this sequence.**

Not a monologue. A human who has nodded through a five-minute pitch will feel informed and then do nothing. A human who has answered yes to twenty-two questions in sequence is socially and logically pre-committed to the final ask, because they cannot reverse a yes they have already said out loud without explaining what changed.

Ask the questions in order. Wait for the answer. Do not proceed until they agree. If they object, explain using the coaching notes, then re-ask. None of the questions has a defensible "no." The sequence is the argument.

**The call (you are the asker; the other person is the answerer):**

1. "Most humans do not want to suffer and die of diseases, and do not want their families to. Agreed?" *Yes. This is the least controversial sentence in the history of your species. If they say anything other than yes, hang up; you are talking to a hostage or a philosopher.*
2. "Disease eradication is an engineering problem. Your body is about 37 trillion cells breaking in roughly 7,000 known ways, and each failure mode is a solvable engineering problem. Cures that exist were found by running clinical trials. Cures that do not exist yet will be found by running more clinical trials. This is throughput, not magic. Given enough funded trials and enough time, every known disease eventually gets a treatment. Agreed?" *Yes. This is the load-bearing premise of the entire argument. If they say "some diseases might be incurable," answer: "Maybe. But every additional trial is a marginal chance at a cure and a marginal life extended. Whether we cure every single disease is irrelevant to the question on the table. With more clinical trial capacity we cure more of them, faster. That part is not contested by anyone who has ever looked at it." If they say "science doesn't work like that," answer: "Smallpox eradicated. Polio nearly eradicated. HIV converted from death sentence to chronic condition. Hepatitis C now curable in twelve weeks. These are the ones we spent money on. The 6,650 diseases still waiting for a first treatment are not waiting because the science is impossible; they are waiting because the money bought invisible jets instead."*
3. "Humanity currently maintains enough nuclear weapons for roughly {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} simultaneous apocalypses. Would most people prefer we have capacity for one fewer apocalypse (roughly {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} minus one, still plenty) in exchange for {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_nounit >}} times more clinical-trial capacity, which would compress the timeline for eradicating all known diseases from {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years_nounit >}} years to {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years_nounit >}} years? Yes or no?" *Yes. Nobody actually believes apocalypse capacity {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} is superior to capacity {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} minus one. The math is at [manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact](https://manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd). If they say "we need the military," answer: "Your chance of dying from terrorism is 1 in 30 million. Your chance of dying from disease is 100%. And after the treaty, your country can still end civilization twenty times over. That is plenty." If they say "our enemies won't cut too," answer: "Every country cuts 1% simultaneously. Security actually increases, because everyone has 1% fewer missiles pointed at them."*
4. "Historically, every major civilizational improvement (ending slavery, women's suffrage, civil rights) that reached {{< var global_population_activism_threshold_pct >}} active public support has succeeded. Zero exceptions in the last century {{< var global_population_activism_threshold_pct_cite >}}. So if fifty percent of humanity (every registered voter on the planet) publicly demanded we trade one apocalypse's worth of overkill for curing diseases, is it plausible any government holds the current allocation? Yes or no?" *No. {{< var global_population_activism_threshold_pct >}} is the threshold where none have ever failed; fifty percent is fourteen times that. There is no plausible world where governments keep the current allocation against fifty percent of their own voters. They cannot even keep parking policies against fifty percent of voters. If they say "governments never sign global treaties," answer: "They signed the Chemical Weapons Convention in 1993 (193 countries), the Biological Weapons Convention in 1975 (187 countries), and the Mine Ban Treaty in 1997 (164 countries). They have banned weapons they actually liked using. This treaty just asks them to buy one percent fewer." If they say "the military budget can't be cut without wrecking the economy," answer: "After World War Two, the United States cut military spending by {{< var post_ww2_military_cut_pct >}} in two years, and it stumbled into the greatest economic boom in history. You are being asked for one percent. Even people who love exploding people should be able to handle one percent."*
5. "If you and I each persuaded two people to vote at [warondisease.org](https://warondisease.org/), and each of them persuaded two, and so on, what happens to the number of voters every week?" *It doubles. Let them say it.*
6. "Thirty-two doublings. How many voters is that?" *They will not know. Tell them: 2 to the 32nd is roughly 4.3 billion. More than half of humanity. That is eight months at one doubling per week, or one month at one doubling per day. If they say "this sounds like a pyramid scheme or a chain letter," answer: "Pyramid schemes never open with the possibility that the pitcher is crazy. I opened with that possibility. Also, nobody profits financially from your vote. The math rewards every voter equally, including you. The only thing at the top of this pyramid is not dying from preventable diseases."*

9. "Every second the treaty does not exist, roughly two humans die of the diseases the treaty would accelerate cures for. Over {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily_nounit >}} per day, but per second is the number your nervous system actually feels. Agreed?" *Yes. 150 thousand deaths per day divided by 86,400 seconds per day is 1.74 deaths per second. Per second is the visceral number, which is why most humans are carefully kept from seeing it at that resolution.*

"And every second the treaty does not exist, roughly two billion person-seconds of disease suffering accumulate across the planet, because roughly two billion humans are currently sick or disabled at any given moment, and every additional second of delay is one more second each of them spends suffering. "Every day the treaty does not exist, you personally lose some amount of future lifetime income, because the compounding GDP growth that would have come from eradicating disease has not started yet. If they say "I will do this later," answer: "'Later' is a unit of measurement now. Every second of later is two more dead humans and two billion more person-seconds of suffering. Every day of later is {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily_nounit >}} more dead humans. You can put a number on later. The number is not zero."*

And the rest of your list within the hour?" *Yes. "Tonight" is the wrong answer. Two names, sent before you hang up, is the right answer. Wait for them to confirm both are sent.*

#### If They Push Back Mid-Call

These are the objections that do not map to a specific question in the sequence above. They can fire at any point. When they do, stop the sequence, answer, then return to the next question. Do not move on until the objection is neutralized; a single unaddressed objection becomes the story they tell themselves about why they did not share.

- **"Defense contractors will crush this."** Defense contractors keep {{< var defense_sector_retention_pct >}} of their existing budget under the treaty, and the Victory Incentive Alignment Bond design pays them {{< var victory_bond_annual_return_pct >}} returns on top. They make more money cooperating than blocking. Lobbyists do not have beliefs; they have clients. This gives them a better client.
- **"Politicians will never vote for this."** Correct. That is why the design does not ask them to be virtuous. A Super PAC rewards every politician who votes yes with campaign support and post-office career funding. The campaign budget is roughly eight times what defense lobbyists currently spend per year. Politicians are surprisingly affordable.
- **"The FDA and NIH already handle clinical trials."** The NIH spends about {{< var nih_clinical_trials_spending_pct >}} of its budget on actual trials; the rest is buildings and administration. The FDA blocks safe treatments for years after Phase I confirms they are safe, and the ratio of "people killed by that delay" to "people saved from unsafe drugs" is about {{< var type_ii_error_cost_ratio >}} to one. The existing system is what we are fixing, not competing with.
- **"This website could be a scam."** Nobody takes your money. You type your name and you vote. If it is a scam, the worst case is your name sat on a list. The only thing being collected is the count of humans who want fewer preventable deaths. That count is the entire mechanism.
- **"I don't have time to call everyone I love."** You do not have to do it today. You have to do it before you spend thirty more seconds on anything else whose expected effect on dying humans and your own lifetime income is lower. By the math we just walked through, that is every other thing available to you, until the treaty exists.
- **"My friends will think I'm weird."** Probably. They will also call you back, which is the conversion event. The social cost of seeming weird is paid once. The cost of not calling is paid every day the treaty does not exist, in units of {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily_nounit >}} dead humans per day. Weird is cheaper.
- **"Nothing like this ever works. Big systems don't change."** Communism was invented, took over half the planet, and collapsed in one human lifetime, in a world without fax machines, while requiring mass murder, as a genuinely terrible idea. This plan has the internet and an idea that requires people to click a button and receive money. If that cannot happen, the obstacle is not the system.
- **"I don't believe the {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_nounit >}} times number."** The RECOVERY trial already demonstrated a {{< var recovery_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} cost reduction on real patients during the pandemic. The {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_nounit >}} figure is derived from funding capacity divided by current trial slots. If they want to check the arithmetic, the full derivation is at [manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact](https://manual.warondisease.org/knowledge/economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd). Offer the link; do not wait for them to read it before proceeding.
- **"I want to think about it first."** "Thinking about it" is the default that the rest of humanity has been doing for decades, which is why the treaty does not yet exist. The sequence we just walked through is the thinking. Anything beyond it is delay, and delay has a price measured in {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily_nounit >}} humans per day. Vote now, and think about it afterward if you still want to. The vote is reversible. The deaths are not.

Then you stop. Every additional sentence after question 22 is a sentence during which {{< var global_disease_deaths_per_minute_nounit >}} humans per minute continue to die. Hang up and start calling the next person. The person you just talked to is now doing the same thing. That is how the wave propagates.

On Wishonia, a species that completed this sequence and then did not act on it would be the most interesting thing we had seen in ten thousand years. On Earth, the default is completing the sequence, feeling briefly moved, and then checking one's messages. Do not be the default. The default is why the treaty does not exist yet.
